subject: english
label: WASSCE May/June 2012 — Paper 1 (Objective)
note: All 100 objective items, answered. Items where the scan is damaged are marked "check".

items.q: Marlu did atone for the loss of his brother's trousers by giving him a new watch.
items.why: "Atone" means to make up for a wrong. The gift of a new watch is the compensation.

items.q: As he listened to my story his face remained inscrutable.
items.why: Inscrutable describes a face that gives nothing away.

items.q: The director gave a very emotional speech at the graduation.
items.why: An emotional speech is charged with feeling; "passionate" is the closest synonym.

items.q: My father lives a humdrum life in the village.
items.why: Humdrum means dull and repetitive.

items.q: There has always been considerable rift between the two parties.
items.why: A rift is a serious disagreement.

items.q: Farnatta believed that the murder of her brother was premeditated.
items.why: "Premeditated" means thought out in advance.

items.q: The little rabbit in the grass looks timid.
items.why: Timid means easily frightened; "shy" is the nearest option.

items.q: Karma's father jailed him for larceny.
items.why: Larceny is theft of personal property — not armed robbery.

items.q: There were several allegations made in the report against your client.
items.why: An allegation is a claim or assertion, usually unproven.

items.q: When the criminal case came up, the police were filled with apprehension.
items.why: Apprehension here means anxious fear, not "arrest".

items.q: The food at Martha's restaurant is very palatable.
items.why: Palatable means pleasant to taste.

items.q: The report on the accident was said to be subjective.
items.a: D — full of the writer's personal feelings
items.why: Subjective = based on personal opinion rather than fact.

items.q: The businessman says that most of his customers are creditworthy, but few are ____.
items.why: Creditworthy (able to pay) contrasts with insolvent (unable to pay debts).

items.q: Her song was much more melancholy in tone while Miatta's was ____.
items.why: The "while" signals contrast; melancholy means sad.

items.q: There are more peaceful people in our club than ____ ones.
items.why: The scanned word is damaged; "dubious" is the only option that can carry a negative contrast.

items.q: Four of the member countries accepted the report while one ____ it.
items.why: The opposite of accepted is rejected.

items.q: He does not know the difference between compliments and ____.
items.why: A compliment praises; an insult wounds — direct opposites.

items.q: Private issues should not be discussed in the ____.
items.why: Private contrasts with public.

items.q: Bertha is indifferent about her school work but Korto is ____.
items.why: Indifferent (uninterested) contrasts with concerned.

items.q: The crowd assembled for the meeting but the police ____ them.
items.why: Assembled (gathered) is reversed by dispersed (scattered).

items.q: Our discussion yesterday was much more inspiring unlike the past ones which were ____.
items.why: Inspiring contrasts with bland (dull, unstimulating).

items.q: We inhale oxygen and ____ carbon dioxide.
items.why: Inhale breathes in; exhale breathes out.

items.q: English Language is compulsory but Literature is ____.
items.why: Compulsory contrasts with optional.

items.q: In the absence of orderliness there is ____.
items.why: Orderliness contrasts with confusion/disorder.

items.q: Kortuma and his family are always at loggerheads.
items.why: At loggerheads = in persistent conflict.

items.q: The judge admonished the witness not to beat about the bush.
items.a: D — to go straight to the point
items.why: Beating about the bush means avoiding the main issue.

items.q: The boy walked at a snail's pace.
items.why: A snail moves very slowly; the image transfers to the walking.

items.q: Academically, our science class is second to none in the community.
items.why: Second to none = nothing ranks above it.

items.q: The coordinator needs to throw more light on his recent statement.
items.why: Shedding light on something means clarifying it.

items.q: My friend Amelia is a snake in the grass.
items.why: A hidden snake strikes unexpectedly — an image of concealed treachery.

items.q: Our union should not encourage yellow journalism.
items.why: Yellow journalism = reporting that exaggerates for sensation.

items.q: If you give Alfred an inch he takes a mile.
items.why: The idiom describes exploiting a small concession.

items.q: We had doubts about Etta's leadership but she rose up to the occasion.
items.why: Rising to the occasion means meeting a challenge successfully.

items.q: My grandmother's house ____ so we have to stay at a hotel until the painting is completed.
items.why: Present continuous passive: the house is receiving the action now.

items.q: "I hope that you ____ all that I have told you," the old man told the boy.
items.why: The hope concerns a future state, so the future tense is required.

items.q: Students with good behaviour usually ____ well in their lessons.
items.why: The plural subject "students" takes the base form "do".

items.q: Of all the languages in the world, English is ____.
items.why: Comparing more than two things requires the superlative.

items.q: After all the criticisms Henry dare not ____ any more mistakes.
items.why: "Dare not" is followed by the bare infinitive.

items.q: You are going with your friend to the party, ____?
items.why: The tag mirrors "are" and reverses polarity.

items.q: I ____ my parents last Sunday but I went out of town.
items.why: Expresses an unfulfilled obligation in the past.

items.q: Amelia left the party early, so she ____ the fight.
items.why: "Did not" takes the base form, not the past tense.

items.q: The striking workers refused ____ work today.
items.why: "Refuse" is followed by the to-infinitive.

items.q: The culprits ____ to jail after the trial.
items.why: Plural subject + past passive: "were sent".

items.q: Most of the spectators ____ see the game.
items.why: "Hardly" is already negative; adding "not" creates a double negative.

items.q: Albertha was ____ that she was soon promoted.
items.why: "Such a + adjective + noun + that" is the correct pattern.

items.q: When we entered the hall, the concert ____.
items.why: Past perfect marks an action completed before another past action.

items.q: Having ____ a deal with the construction company, the manager was pleased.
items.why: Perfect participle needs the past participle "struck".

items.q: Mr. Massaquoi's car did not start; ____ he was late for work today.
items.why: The second clause is a result of the first.

items.q: He accused the janitor ____ his book.
items.why: The fixed pattern is "accuse somebody of (doing) something".

items.q: The number of malaria cases in the county ____ increasing.
items.why: "The number of" is singular, so it takes "has".

items.q: Uncle Samakai will go for a short training course before ____ his new job.
items.why: "Take up a job" = begin it; the preposition "before" takes the -ing form.

items.q: Solomon completed the exercise, ____ he was sick.
items.why: The clauses contrast, so a concessive connector is needed.

items.q: We worked hard during our final year, ____?
items.why: The statement is affirmative past, so the tag is negative past.

items.q: The patient is gradually recovering ____ his illness.
items.why: The fixed collocation is "recover from an illness".

items.q: If he ____ the election, he would have become a member of the legislature.
items.why: Third conditional: "if + had + past participle … would have + past participle".

items.q: "I ____ be able to go to the concert," she said uncertainly.
items.why: "Uncertainly" points to possibility, not obligation or certainty.

items.q: ____ the long distance I ran, I never got tired.
items.why: "In spite of" takes a noun phrase ("the long distance"), matching the structure.

items.q: Which of the two cars is the ____?
items.why: Only two cars are compared, so the comparative is required.

items.q: I am not ____ in learning Chinese.
items.why: "Interested in" describes the person; "interesting" describes the thing.

items.q: Did anyone ____ to the principal about our project?
items.why: After "did", the base form is used.

items.q: Many children in Liberia take care of ____.
items.why: "Theirselves" is not a word; the correct reflexive is "themselves".

items.q: The audience described the president's message as ____.
items.why: The message causes interest, so the -ing adjective is correct.

items.q: There are several courses offered and you may select ____ course you desire.
items.why: A free choice among things takes "whichever".

items.q: The hotel at the stadium is about ____.
items.why: The standard measure phrase is "three stories high".

items.q: Because of some misunderstanding, the workers ____ strike action.
items.why: The scan reads "resulted to", but the idiomatic verb is "resort to". Choose the past-tense "to"-form.

items.q: Miatta spends most of her time reading, writing letters and ____ to her friends on the phone.
items.why: All items in the list must share the same -ing form.

items.q: All of my friends love to eat, dance and ____ funny jokes.
items.why: The list follows "love to", so each verb is a bare infinitive.

items.q: The game was ____ enjoyable that they did not want to leave.
items.why: "So + adjective + that" expresses result.

items.q: If she had not been smart, the thief ____ away with her money.
items.why: Third conditional result clause: "would have + past participle".

items.q: We saw the young man suddenly ____ from the truck.
items.why: Verbs of perception ("saw") take the bare infinitive.

items.q: We need to write a letter and ____ the manager for his contribution.
items.why: "Need to write … and thank" keeps the bare infinitive after "to".

items.q: Liberian children should strive ____ their parents.
items.why: "Strive to + verb" is the correct pattern.

items.q: Mr. Jalebah led a ____ delegation to the Council meeting.
items.why: A compound adjective before a noun is singular: "a three-man delegation". The option duplicates "a"; the word itself is right.

items.q: Musa is intelligent; he is quick ____.
items.why: The adjective "quick" takes the to-infinitive.

items.q: Your suit is ____ mine.
items.why: Comparison between two items uses "more … than".

items.q: We should learn ____ kindly to one another.
items.why: "Learn to + verb" is the required pattern.

items.q: Unauthorized persons ____ the gate during working hours.
items.why: "Dare not" takes the bare infinitive and needs no auxiliary.

items.q: The supervisor of schools ____ our school before.
items.why: "Before" with "has" forms the present perfect, which fits the completed auxiliary in the stem.

items.q: I ____ in the track team next week.
items.why: Future continuous describes an activity in progress at a future time.

items.q: He had fever so he ____ in bed all day yesterday.
items.why: The past tense of "lie" (to recline) is "lay".

items.q: The two parties in the dispute agreed ____.
items.why: "Agree to + verb" for accepting a proposal.

items.q: We have not seen the box ____.
items.a: C — in which we kept the golden key
items.why: The relative clause needs a preposition + which, and the golden key is what was kept.

items.q: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
items.a: Options are illegible in the scan — check against your printed paper.
items.why: All four options are corrupted in the text layer.

items.q: … obtained a ____ from the ____ office to enable him travel …
items.why: A passport is the travel document that enables international travel.

items.q: … from the ____ office …
items.why: Among the options, a passport is issued through the Foreign Affairs/immigration office.

items.q: … working at the American ____ helped him …
items.why: The American Embassy is the natural institution.

items.q: … to obtain a ____ for his trip.
items.why: A visa is the entry permit attached to a passport.

items.q: He later ____ his ticket from a ____ …
items.why: Tickets are purchased; the past tense fits the narrative.

items.q: … his ticket from a ____ …
items.why: Travel agencies sell tickets.

items.q: … and ____ his ____ for July 2011.
items.why: One confirms a booking, not insures or assigns it.

items.q: … and confirmed his ____ for July 2011.
items.why: A flight is confirmed for a date.

items.q: I accompanied him to the airport and reported at the ____ …
items.why: Passengers check in at the departure desk.

items.q: … for the ____ formalities.
items.why: Departure formalities precede boarding.

items.q: I watched the planes ____ and ____.
items.why: Planes take off and land.
The paired action to "take off" is "land".

items.q: After inspection of his passport and luggage he was issued a ____.
items.why: A boarding pass is issued after check-in.

items.q: I saw the plane ____ into space.
items.why: Zooming conveys rapid upward movement.

items.q: He had a smooth ____ to the USA.
items.why: A journey by air is a flight.

items.q: His ____ took him to Accra …
items.why: A route is the path a journey follows.

items.q: … where he ____ for three hours.
items.why: A stop-over is a brief break in a longer journey.

subject: english
label: WASSCE May/June 2012 — Paper 2 (Essay, Comprehension, Summary)
note: Essay questions have no single right answer, so these are model plans and full model answers for the comprehension and summary.

items.q: According to the passage, what difference in reading speed does the author show between poor readers and highly educated readers?
items.a: Highly educated adults vary their speed according to the material and their purpose in reading, whereas poor readers keep the same speed whatever they read.
steps: The passage opens by saying adults, even highly educated ones, "vary greatly in the speed and efficiency of their reading".
It then says some read slowly and others rush and must go back.
The key contrast is with "poor readers", who "may lack the ability to vary their manner of reading according to the type of reading matter".
So the difference is flexibility of speed, not simply fast versus slow.
items.tip: Answer the exact question asked. Saying "educated readers are faster" is wrong — the passage says they vary.

items.q: Why does the author think that proof-reading is very difficult for most people?
items.a: Because people are accustomed to overlooking the exact shape and order of letters and words, which is precisely what proof-reading requires them to notice.
steps: Locate the sentence about proof-reading.
It says the reader must notice "not so much the meaning ... as the exact shape and order of letters and words".
It then gives the reason: "since they are accustomed to overlooking such details".
Join the two: the habit of reading for meaning makes close attention to form difficult.
items.tip: The answer is a cause, so begin with "Because …" and quote the causal clause.

items.q: What does the phrase "take in the whole of it" mean in the passage?
items.a: To understand and absorb the entire content of the material.
items.why: It is used of reading "more difficult material, with the intention of taking in the whole of it" — that is, grasping all of it, not skimming.

items.q: Give the meaning of "regress" as used in the passage.
items.a: Go back over what has already been read.
items.why: Context: readers who "dash along too quickly and then have to regress" — they must return to an earlier point.

items.q: Give the meaning of "skim" as used in the passage.
items.a: Read very quickly to get only the general idea.
items.why: Context: "He may be able to skim a page, pick up a word or two here and there, and gain a general idea".

items.q: Give the meaning of "proof-reading" as used in the passage.
items.a: Reading a text very slowly and carefully in order to detect misprints.
items.why: The passage defines it as reading that "necessitates careful attention to detail" in order "to detect misprints in a sample print".

items.q: Give the meaning of "misprint" as used in the passage.
items.a: A printing error — a word or letter printed wrongly.
items.why: Proof-reading exists to detect misprints, so the word names the error itself.

items.q: According to the passage, what is the purpose of advertising?
items.a: To persuade people to buy the products that advertisers have for sale.
items.why: The passage opens: "Advertisers have something to sell and they use a number of ways to persuade us to buy their products."

items.q: What aspect of human nature do advertisers use to persuade people to buy products?
items.a: The feelings and fears common to nearly everyone — the need for security, popularity, health, success and attractiveness.
items.why: The second paragraph lists exactly these: security, popularity, health, success and attractiveness.

items.q: Give an appropriate title for the passage.
items.a: The Art of Advertising (accept: Advertising and Human Behaviour; How Advertisers Persuade Us).
steps: A title must cover the whole passage, not one paragraph.
The passage is about advertisers exploiting common emotions.
Keep it short — a phrase, not a sentence.
Do not simply copy the first line.
items.tip: Titles are usually noun phrases with no full stop.

items.q: Letter: your pen pal abroad asks about recreation facilities in your country. Describe one facility that would interest him.
items.a: Model plan for an informal letter of about 150 words.
steps: Address and date at the top right; salutation "Dear Kofi,".
Paragraph 1: acknowledge his letter and state why you are writing.
Paragraph 2: name the facility and say where it is (for example the national sports stadium).
Paragraph 3: describe what it offers — swimming pool, tennis courts, football pitch, gymnasium, restaurant.
Paragraph 4: explain why it would interest him — major matches, coaching sessions, chances to meet people.
Paragraph 5: practical details — opening hours, entry fee, how to get there.
Close with "Yours sincerely," and your first name.
items.tip: An informal letter still needs paragraphs. One solid paragraph per idea scores better than one block of text.

items.q: Letter: as youth leader of your district, write to the district representative about major development needs and how he/she could assist.
items.a: Model plan for a formal letter of about 150 words.
steps: Your address and date; the representative's official address below it.
Salutation "Dear Sir/Madam,"; a clear subject line.
Opening: state who you are and the body you represent.
Body: three numbered needs — for example feeder roads, a health centre, and a skills-training centre for the youth.
For each need, say briefly what it costs the community and what specific help you want.
Close by inviting a meeting; sign "Yours faithfully," with your full name.
items.tip: Formal letters use "Yours faithfully" with "Dear Sir/Madam". "Yours sincerely" belongs with a named recipient.

items.q: Article for the school magazine: "The Importance of Good Appearance".
items.a: Model plan for an essay of about 250 words.
steps: Title centred, then a byline (your name).
Introduction: define appearance as dress, grooming and bearing — not beauty.
Point 1: first impressions are formed in seconds and are hard to reverse.
Point 2: good appearance builds self-confidence and affects how you perform.
Point 3: it signals respect for others and for the occasion.
Point 4: it opens doors in interviews and public life.
Counterpoint: appearance is not character — warn against judging people by dress alone.
Conclusion: neatness is within everyone's reach, regardless of income.
items.tip: An article needs a title and byline. Marks are usually set aside for them.

items.q: You witnessed a street demonstration in which people were injured and property damaged. Give a vivid description of the scene.
items.a: Model plan for a descriptive essay of about 250 words.
steps: Open in the middle of the action, not with background — a description, not a story.
Use the senses: chanting and whistles (sound), tear gas (smell and sight), dust and heat (feel).
Move in a clear order — from the front of the crowd outward, or from beginning to aftermath.
Choose three or four sharp details rather than listing everything: a fallen banner, a shattered windscreen, a bleeding trader.
Use strong verbs and similes, but do not overdo the adjectives.
Close on a single striking image that fixes the mood.
items.tip: A description is judged on sensory detail and organisation, not on plot. Do not turn it into a story with a hero.

items.q: Write an imaginary story which justifies the saying, "Hope is the last thing we lose."
items.a: Model plan for a narrative essay of about 250 words.
steps: Establish a character with a clear goal and a mounting obstacle.
Let the situation worsen in two or three stages so the loss feels real.
Show the moment of near-despair — this is where "hope is the last thing" must be earned.
Introduce one small, believable opportunity rather than a miraculous rescue.
Show the character acting on it, and let the outcome follow logically.
Return explicitly to the saying in the final line, but do not preach.
Keep one tense throughout — past tense is safest.
items.tip: The examiner marks whether the story actually illustrates the saying. A story that only mentions it at the end without demonstrating it loses the content marks.

subject: english
label: WASSCE May/June 2016 — Paper 2 (Comprehension & Summary)
note: Model answers worked from the passage printed in the paper. The PDF contains no marking scheme.

items.q: Why did the writer's father warn the boys against going out at night?
items.a: Because recent happenings had shown that it was unsafe to go out at night.
items.why: The passage states the reason directly: "since recent happenings had shown that it was unsafe".

items.q: Quote a phrase in the second paragraph which shows that the teacher's house was not far from the writer's own.
steps: Scan paragraph 2 only — the question restricts you to it.
Look for a comparison of distance.
"A stone's throw" is an idiom for a very short distance.
Quote it exactly, in quotation marks.
items.tip: When a question says "quote", copy the words verbatim. Paraphrasing scores zero even if the meaning is right.

items.q: What enabled the teacher to discover the boys?
items.a: The powerful headlights of his approaching car lit up the scene, and he spotted them.
items.why: The passage says "the powerful headlights of an approaching car warned us" and "he had already spotted us".

items.q: Describe what led to the writer's injury.
items.a: In his haste to get down from the mango tree after being spotted, he lost his balance and fell heavily, injuring his arm.
steps: Sequence the cause: being spotted → panic → hurried descent.
State the loss of balance.
State the fall and the specific injury (his arm).
Keep it to the causal chain the question asks for.

items.q: Why did the writer's father refuse to open the door?
items.a: He believed his son was sleeping peacefully in his room, so he thought the teacher was mistaken.
items.why: His reply is "My son is sleeping peacefully in his room" — he was unaware of the boy's absence.

items.q: "…an instant alarm…" (i) What is the grammatical name given to this expression? (ii) What is its function?
items.a: (i) Noun phrase. (ii) Object of the verb "raised".
steps: The head word is "alarm" — a noun, so the whole expression is a noun phrase.
"Instant" is a modifier, not the head.
Ask what the phrase does in "The teacher raised an instant alarm": it receives the action of "raised".
Therefore it functions as the object of the verb.
items.tip: Name the phrase by its head word, then state its function by its job in the sentence — two separate marks.

items.q: "…like the wind…" (i) What figure of speech is contained in this expression? (ii) What does it mean?
items.a: (i) Simile. (ii) It means very fast / at great speed.
items.why: The comparison uses "like", which is the marker of a simile.

items.q: Give another word or phrase that can replace each of: recent, delicious, stealthily, approaching, spotted, verify.
items.a: recent → latest/current; delicious → tasty/mouth-watering; stealthily → secretly/quietly; approaching → coming/nearing; spotted → saw/noticed; verify → confirm/check.
steps: Replace each word in its original sentence and check the meaning still fits.
Keep the same part of speech: "spotted" is a verb here, so the replacement must be a verb.
Do not simply repeat the word with a suffix.
One word or short phrase per item.
items.tip: "As used in the passage" means context decides. A dictionary synonym that breaks the sentence earns nothing.

items.q: In four sentences, one for each, summarize the factors that have prompted the rapid increase in world population.
items.a: Improved medical care and available drugs have cut death rates and raised life expectancy. The spread of education has created awareness of health and welfare and dispelled harmful myths. Better farming practices and tools have increased the food supply and reduced hunger. Relative security and the absence of major wars have reduced war-related deaths.
steps: Identify the four factor paragraphs: health, education, nutrition, security.
One sentence per factor — do not merge two factors into a sentence.
Use your own words; lift only technical terms.
Keep each sentence short and complete.
items.tip: The instruction "one for each" is a hard constraint. Five sentences where four are required can lose marks even if the content is right.

items.q: In two sentences, one for each, summarize what is likely to follow the continuing rapid population growth.
items.a: Gross over-population may leave too little arable land to produce enough food. Rapid growth may also cause environmental degradation through the waste that homes and industries generate.
steps: The final paragraph names two dangers.
First danger: insufficient arable land for food production.
Second danger: pollution and environmental degradation from waste.
Write each as one sentence, in your own words.
items.tip: Summary answers must be continuous prose — bullet points and lifted sentences are penalised.

subject: english
label: WASSCE May/June 2016 — Paper 1 (Objective)
note: All 80 objective items across Sections 1–6 (antonyms, sentence completion, interpretation, synonyms, structure, cloze).

items.q: That road which used to be wide now appears ____ because of the new drainage.
items.why: Wide is opposed by narrow; the drainage has taken part of the road's width.

items.q: In the past, any person who angered the gods was made to ____ them.
items.why: To anger is to provoke; to appease is to pacify — the required opposite.

items.q: Rather than being sensitive to the plight of the workers, the manager remained ____.
items.why: "Rather than" marks contrast with sensitive; indifferent means showing no concern.

items.q: A keen student makes progress but the ____ one hardly does well.
items.why: Keen means eager and actively interested; the contrast is with inactive. "Reluctant" describes unwillingness rather than lack of activity, and the sentence is about effort producing progress.

items.q: Unlike you, I thought the message was quite ____, not ambiguous.
items.why: Ambiguous (having more than one meaning) is opposed by clear.

items.q: Good policies alleviate poverty whereas bad ones ____.
items.why: "Whereas" marks contrast; alleviate (ease) is opposed by aggravate (make worse).

items.q: One expects books in a library to be well ____, not jumbled.
items.why: Jumbled (mixed up) is opposed by arranged (put in order).

items.q: Despite everything, I chose to keep rather than ____ the secret.
items.why: The direct opposite of keep a secret is reveal it.

items.q: Though the teachers ____ the idea, the principal was averse to it.
items.why: Averse (opposed) is contrasted by "though", so the teachers must have favoured it — welcomed.

items.q: It is only natural to feel nervous when you first take the stage but you soon become ____.
items.why: Nervous is opposed by composed (calm and self-controlled).

items.q: Don't tell me you're ____ enough to believe his lies.
items.why: Naive means easily deceived through lack of experience — exactly the sense needed.

items.q: The members of parliament tabled an ____ to the constitution.
items.why: An amendment is a formal change to a document; "adjustment" is too informal for a constitution.

items.q: His ____ to violent video games is something to worry about.
items.why: Addiction implies a harmful dependency; dedication and attachment are neutral or positive.

items.q: Most people think that ____ punishment should be abolished, even in murder cases.
items.why: Capital punishment is the death penalty — the only kind abolished even for murder.

items.q: The President made a ____ appeal for calm in the face of the crisis.
items.why: A passionate appeal is an earnest, strongly felt one — the natural collocation.

items.q: What I gave you was supposed to ____ your monthly earnings.
items.why: To augment is to add to or increase — the precise register here.

items.q: The boy's parents ____ a sigh of relief when he was found.
items.why: The fixed collocation is "heave a sigh of relief".

items.q: We ____ the meeting indefinitely because we could not form a quorum.
items.why: To adjourn is to suspend a meeting without fixing the next date — matching "indefinitely".

items.q: The policeman tried to ____ money from the motorist.
items.why: To extort is to obtain money by threat or force. "Extract" suggests removal, not coercion.

items.q: They were given an ____: either pay the rent or vacate the premises.
items.why: An ultimatum is a final demand with a stated consequence — exactly the two-part structure here.

items.q: My school carried the day in the debate.
items.why: To carry the day is to be victorious.

items.q: We covered much ground at the conference yesterday.
items.why: Covering ground means dealing with a range of topics, not physical space.

items.q: We saw Ada, of all people, dancing.
items.a: D — we were surprised to see Ada dancing
items.why: "Of all people" signals surprise that this particular person did it.

items.q: There are clear indications that Buba backed the wrong horse.
items.why: Backing the wrong horse means supporting a cause or person that loses.

items.q: I knew that they were being economical with the truth.
items.a: C — knew more than they were prepared to say
items.why: Being economical with the truth is withholding part of it, not being ignorant of it.

items.q: My mother wanted to know what was eating him.
items.why: "What is eating someone" is what is troubling or worrying them.

items.q: People who tell lies make me seethe.
items.why: To seethe is to be boiling with anger.

items.q: After several attempts to claim the child, he threw in the towel.
items.why: Throwing in the towel is conceding defeat, from boxing.

items.q: This is their third defeat in a row.
items.why: "In a row" means consecutively, and "their defeat" means they lost rather than won.

items.q: The company has been under siege from the public.
items.why: Under siege here means subjected to sustained public attack, not physically picketed.

items.q: Most people abhor nagging.
items.why: To abhor is to hate intensely; despise is the closest in strength and register.

items.q: I really hope Beatrice would be kind enough to let us stay the night.
items.why: Gracious means showing courtesy and generosity — a better fit for hospitality than merely polite.

items.q: I personally think that the costume is rather outlandish.
items.why: Outlandish means conspicuously unusual or strange.

items.q: He did all he could to fortify the building against attack.
items.why: To fortify is to strengthen against attack, that is, to secure it.

items.q: This is one decision you cannot defend.
items.why: To defend a decision is to justify it.

items.q: He simply disliked his wife's inordinate demands for money.
items.why: Inordinate means beyond reasonable limits.

items.q: Bravery is Victor's most dominant trait.
items.why: Dominant here means most prominent or outstanding.

items.q: It's always better to buy durable products.
items.why: Durable means able to withstand wear — long-lasting. "Permanent" is too absolute.

items.q: Where did this document emanate from?
items.why: To emanate is to come or originate from a source.

items.q: The management applauded the staff for their hard work.
items.why: To applaud figuratively is to praise formally — commended.

items.q: You like ice cream, ____?
items.why: Affirmative present "like" takes the negative tag "don't you".

items.q: I didn't tell my parents about the trip because they would be ____ themselves with worry.
items.why: The idiom is "beside oneself with worry", meaning overwhelmed.

items.q: We arrived just ____ time for the formal opening.
items.why: The idiom is "in time", meaning early enough.

items.q: She claims ____ someone jump over the fence.
items.why: "Claim" takes the to-infinitive, and the event is prior, so the perfect infinitive is required.

items.q: Kofi says he is better at Physics ____.
items.why: Comparison needs "than", and the verb must be included to complete the clause correctly.

items.q: Her shoes are made ____ genuine leather.
items.why: When the material is unchanged in the finished product, the preposition is "of".

items.q: Even after his explanation, I was none the ____.
items.why: The idiom "none the wiser" means still not understanding.

items.q: I spoke to Mary and Peter on the issue but ____ of them took my advice.
items.why: Two people, both failing to act — neither. "Either" would be affirmative.

items.q: We need to ____ for lost time.
items.why: The idiom is "make up for lost time".

items.q: Everyone wants to be the ____ favourite.
items.why: The favourite belongs to the principal, so the possessive falls on principal, and "school" modifies it attributively.

items.q: That haircut makes him ____ in the crowd.
items.why: To stand out is to be conspicuously noticeable.

items.q: The deal ____ because we could not get enough money to finance it.
items.why: A deal that falls through fails to be completed.

items.q: ____ in this town for many years, I can tell you a lot about its people.
items.why: The perfect participle shows the living happened before the present ability to speak.

items.q: I don't believe that any ____ person would do such a thing.
items.why: The adjective "mature" modifies "person"; "matured" is a past participle and "matures" a verb.

items.q: The coach, as well as the players, ____ given fantastic gifts last month.
items.why: With "as well as", the verb agrees with the first subject — "the coach", which is singular.

items.q: If he ____ here, he would do it for free.
items.why: The unreal present conditional uses "were" for all persons.

items.q: Had she told me, I ____ you.
items.why: Inverted third conditional: "Had + past participle … would have + past participle".

items.q: Since his transfer to Banjul, my brother ____ our hometown.
items.why: "Since" with a present result requires the present perfect.

items.q: The Minister ____ Agriculture visited our school today.
items.why: The portfolio is expressed as "Minister of Agriculture".

items.q: I was barely halfway home when darkness ____.
items.why: Darkness "sets in" — begins and settles. "Set off" means depart.

items.q: You must obtain a degree ____ medicine to be a doctor.
items.why: A degree in a subject takes "in".

items.q: We'll buy more but for now, let's just ____ with what we have.
items.why: "Make do with" means manage with what is available.

items.q: They told her that we would solve the problem ____.
items.why: The subject of the clause is "we", so the reflexive must be "ourselves".

items.q: The sport I like ____ is swimming.
items.why: The superlative adverb is needed for liking something above all others.

items.q: If you insist that you are not a tailor, ____ are you?
items.why: The question asks about identity, which requires "who".

items.q: If your grades don't improve, I shall have no option ____ to move you to another school.
items.why: The idiom is "have no option but to do something".

items.q: ____ rather he did not stay.
items.why: The construction is "would rather" + past subjunctive: "I would rather he did not stay".

items.q: Your submission is ____.
items.why: The idiom means irrelevant or beside the point.

items.q: Every one of the boys ____ excited about the picnic.
items.why: "Every one" is singular, so the verb takes -s.

items.q: You ____ be ashamed of yourself for saying such a thing before the principal.
items.why: "Should" expresses moral obligation.

items.q: Displaying his ____ very conspicuously on his neck …
items.why: A doctor wears a stethoscope around the neck.

items.q: … he walked through the ____ …
items.why: A hospital ward is where patients are treated and examined.

items.q: … greeting each of the ____ who greeted him in return.
items.why: The people in a ward being greeted by a doctor are patients.

items.q: His eyes caught a woman on a nearby ____.
items.why: She is lying down and is later wheeled away, so she is on a bed.

items.q: He went closer, held her hand, feeling for her ____.
items.why: Feeling the wrist for a pulse is a standard clinical check.

items.q: … and then carried out some other minor ____.
items.why: Minor examinations are checks; probes and drills are instruments or procedures, not "minor" actions done by hand.

items.q: "Stretcher, stretcher, quickly; take her to the ____!"
items.why: The operating theatre is where surgery is performed, and the next line mentions the operating room.

items.q: Even the ____ who had been supervising her treatment were amazed.
items.why: An ectopic pregnancy is a maternity case, so the staff supervising her treatment are midwives.

items.q: "This is an ectopic pregnancy … The ____ must be taken out promptly."
items.why: In an ectopic pregnancy the foetus develops outside the womb and must be removed.

items.q: Before long, the surgery was completed, ____.
items.why: Surgery of this kind is followed by a blood transfusion; "transfusion" is the only medical noun among the options.

label: WASSCE 2023 — English Language 1 (Objective), Part A
note: Questions 1–50: Lexis and Structure (Sections I–V). The Literature section for this paper is in the next two blocks, both alternatives included.

items.q: The diverse groups became ____ in a common course.
items.why: The underlined word is "diverse" (different); the gap needs its opposite, and "united" is the only option that also fits "in a common course".

items.q: Aku's mood changed from the dismal to the ____.
items.why: Dismal means gloomy; the opposite is ecstatic (joyful).

items.q: The invigorating drinks served at the party made us forget how ____ the trip had been.
items.why: Invigorating gives energy; enervating drains it.

items.q: Whereas tourism is thriving, other local businesses are ____.
items.why: "Whereas" marks the contrast; thriving (growing) opposes declining.

items.q: Although now a renowned doctor, Johnny rose from ____ beginnings.
items.why: A renowned present contrasts with humble origins — the classic "humble beginnings" collocation.

items.q: The efforts to defuse the tension, rather ____ it.
items.why: "Rather" signals the opposite of the intended effect; to defuse is to calm, so the gap needs aggravated (made worse).

items.q: Her condition may worsen rather than ____ if she continues to brood over the incident.
items.why: "Rather than" contrasts with worsen, so the gap needs a word meaning get better.

items.q: Charitable actions can influence ____ people to change.
items.why: Charitable (giving to others) is opposed by selfish.

items.q: No one knows the origin of this group, but we are sure of its ____.
items.why: Origin (beginning) is opposed by demise (end). "Extinction" applies to species, not a group's beginning.

items.q: It is interesting that minute creatures survive alongside ____ ones in the same habitat.
items.why: Minute means tiny; the contrast is with large.

items.q: The students tried every means to secure permission, ____?
items.why: The statement is affirmative past ("tried"), so the tag is negative past.

items.q: At the last P.T.A. meeting, tempers ____ between the parents and the teachers.
items.why: "Tempers rose" — rise is intransitive and its past tense is rose. "Arose" means came into being, which does not fit tempers.

items.q: Every human being has a right ____ education.
items.why: The fixed collocation is "a right to education".

items.q: The article ____ the attention of scholars everywhere.
items.why: "Attract attention" is the correct collocation.

items.q: The building remains an ____ testimony to the ingenuity of ancient architecture.
items.why: An eloquent testimony is a vivid, convincing piece of evidence — a standard collocation.

items.q: The manager said ____ criticisms would work for the good of the company.
items.why: Constructive criticism is the kind intended to improve, which matches "for the good of the company".

items.q: The pastor's honesty is ____ question.
items.why: "Without question" means beyond doubt — the only option that forms a correct idiom here.

items.q: But for the timely intervention of the police, the thief ____ lynched.
items.why: "But for" introduces an unreal past condition, so the result clause takes would have + past participle.

items.q: People ____ the world over are benefitting from technology.
items.why: "People around the world" is the standard phrase; "the world over" is a separate idiom that cannot be doubled.

items.q: In a civilized society, one has the chance to express ____ opinion.
items.why: The subject "one" must be matched by the possessive "one's".

items.q: The school was not surprised that Ama felt dejected at seeing her results.
items.why: Dejected means low in spirits because of a setback; disappointed is the closest.

items.q: Serwaa wonders why Koomson has suddenly become conceited after his promotion.
items.why: Conceited means having an inflated opinion of oneself; haughty is the nearest option.

items.q: The government should arrest quack doctors in the country.
items.why: A quack practises without proper qualification and is therefore fraudulent, not merely uneducated.

items.q: Many people deserted the area because of armed robbers.
items.why: To desert a place is to abandon it.

items.q: Issah has shown much dedication to our cause.
items.why: Dedication and commitment are near synonyms.

items.q: The Minister gets angry when you express your candid opinion.
items.why: Candid means frank and honest. "Open" is tempting but "candid opinion" pairs with honest.

items.q: Stephen's performance in the game was sterling.
items.why: Sterling means excellent or outstanding.

items.q: In 1940, Cape Coast Castle was so fortified that no enemy could attack it.
items.why: To fortify is to strengthen against attack; reinforced is the exact match.

items.q: In some secondary schools, new students are harassed by their prefects.
items.why: Harass means to subject repeatedly to unwanted pressure — troubled is the closest neutral option.

items.q: The chief has gained notoriety for his corrupt activities.
items.why: Notoriety is fame for a bad reason; infamy carries exactly that sense.

items.q: Joan made heavy weather of her new position in the office.
items.why: To make heavy weather of something is to struggle with it unnecessarily.

items.q: Ama told her sister not to be afraid for she has her back always.
items.why: To have someone's back is to support and protect them.

items.q: I have half a mind to apply for this post.
items.a: A — am not sure if I should apply
items.why: "Half a mind" expresses hesitation, not refusal.

items.q: Afi cannot make head or tail of what you are saying.
items.why: Being unable to make head or tail of something is being unable to understand it.

items.q: No matter what difficulty you are facing now, there's always a silver lining at the end.
items.why: A silver lining is the hopeful aspect of a bad situation.

items.q: In the last year in office, the director became a lame duck.
items.why: A lame duck is an office holder whose power has run out. Among these options "was weak" is the closest.

items.q: After he lost his election, Thomas withdrew to the village to lick his wounds.
items.why: Licking one's wounds is recovering after a loss.

items.q: In less than three months, the new MD has managed to bring the rebellious union members into line.
items.a: B — making the union members conform to his dictates
items.why: "Into line" means into obedience or conformity.

items.q: Despite his low wages, Mawuli was able to make ends meet.
items.why: To make ends meet is to live within one's means.

items.q: The building project failed because the company cut corners.
items.a: C — spent less resources on the project
items.why: Cutting corners means doing something cheaply or carelessly to save money or effort.

items.q: Football is a game which pits one ____ against the other.
items.why: Football is played between two teams.

items.q: At ____, each is made up of eleven ____.
items.why: "Kick off" is the fixed football term for the start of a match.

items.q: At kick off, each is made up of eleven ____.
items.why: A team consists of players.

items.q: … whose aim is to win the game by ensuring that they score more ____.
items.why: Football is scored in goals, not baskets, points or runs.

items.q: In order to ensure fairness, there is the ____ whose duty is to insist that …
items.why: The referee officiates a football match (an umpire officiates hockey, cricket or tennis).

items.q: … that the ____ of the game are obeyed.
items.why: "Rules of the game" is the standard collocation.

items.q: On each side of the ____, there is a goal post …
items.why: Football is played on a pitch.

items.q: If any other person touches the ball with the hand, that will be a ____.
items.why: Handling the ball is a foul. It becomes a penalty only inside the goal area, as the next sentence says.

items.q: There is always a reserve ____ which coaches rely on for substitutions.
items.why: Substitutes sit on the bench.

items.q: No football match worth its salt is complete without ____.
items.why: Spectators watch a match; supporters are a subset of them, and "without spectators" is the general statement.

subject: english
label: WASSCE 2020 — English Language 1 (Objective), Part A
note: Questions 1–50: Lexis and Structure (Sections I–V). The Literature section for this paper is in the next two blocks, both alternatives included.

items.q: Geraldine is very courteous but her brother, Gerald, is unbelievably ____.
items.why: Courteous (polite) is opposed by impolite. Arrogant and snobbish are not direct opposites of courteous.

items.q: Whilst Lydia became ____ in the course of the contest, Lena was confident.
items.why: "Whilst" marks contrast with confident; jittery means nervous.

items.q: We thought Jane was the instigator of the take-over; it turned out that she was rather the ____.
items.why: An instigator starts trouble; a troubleshooter resolves it. The other options are not opposites.

items.q: When they appeared before the disciplinary committee, Rex was unrepentant but Ray was ____.
items.why: Unrepentant (showing no regret) is opposed by remorseful (full of regret).

items.q: Mama thought what I had done was smart but Dad said it was ____.
items.why: Smart (clever) is opposed by dumb (stupid).

items.q: Question 6 — the sentence did not survive OCR in this scan.
items.a: Cannot be determined from this copy — check your printed paper.
items.why: Only the tail of the sentence and the four options were recovered.

items.q: Instead of being gentle with the frightened child, Tom was rather ____.
items.why: "Instead of" signals contrast with gentle; harsh is the direct opposite.

items.q: I felt very agitated yet I maintained a ____ demeanour.
items.why: "Yet" marks contrast with agitated; calm is the opposite.

items.q: Adding much salt to food at table is ____ to the heart, not beneficial.
items.why: The "not beneficial" clause confirms a negative word; "injurious to" is the correct collocation.

items.q: The sound from Larry's recorder was ____ rather than audible.
items.why: "Rather than audible" needs a word meaning hard to hear; muffled fits.

items.q: We shall overcome ____ how difficult it is.
items.why: "No matter how" is the correct concessive pattern.

items.q: Jemima will be here ____ a minute.
items.why: Future time is expressed with "in a minute".

items.q: The ambulance sped ____ the hill.
items.why: To speed down a hill is the natural collocation; "downwards" would need "the hill" handled differently.

items.q: You ____ a scratch on your neck the last time we met.
items.why: "The last time we met" fixes a past point, so the simple past is required.

items.q: He ____ they should be punished immediately.
items.why: Third-person singular subject takes "thinks"; the present tense suits the general statement.

items.q: ____ midnight, Tom fell asleep.
items.why: "By midnight" means no later than midnight, which fits falling asleep.

items.q: Elorm and Jacob were then ____ war with each other.
items.why: The fixed phrase is "at war with".

items.q: Though Tay had heard their cries for help, he ____ them.
items.why: The past perfect "had heard" requires a simple past in the main clause.

items.q: Ali and Maria are good friends; they seldom ____.
items.why: "Seldom" is a present-tense frequency adverb, so the base form is used with a plural subject.

items.q: Kennedy and Portia ____ live in Accra.
items.why: "Used to + verb" expresses a past state that no longer holds.

items.q: Mother's message was motivational; it gingered the children to work hard.
items.why: Something that gingers people into action inspires them.

items.q: I have a hunch that the programme will not go well.
items.why: A hunch is a feeling or suspicion not yet proven.

items.q: Desmond admonished his people not to go to war.
items.why: In this context admonish means to warn earnestly; "reproved" would imply past fault.

items.q: Parliamentary proceedings have been adjourned until January.
items.why: To adjourn is to suspend or postpone.

items.q: What the professor said was alien to all his students.
items.why: Alien means strange or unfamiliar.

items.q: The unwholesome practice is anathema to decent people.
items.why: Anathema is something intensely detested; "a curse" is the closest option.

items.q: When Joanita was declared winner, pandemonium broke out.
items.why: Pandemonium is wild disorder.

items.q: The subject of sanitation was accentuated at the meeting because of its importance.
items.why: To accentuate is to give emphasis to.

items.q: When the wild dog attacked the puppies, Cecil throttled it.
items.why: To throttle is to seize by the throat.

items.q: Little Simon was given a drug to suppress his hyperactivity.
items.why: To suppress here means to bring under control, not to crush or conquer.

items.q: Ever since Uche disgraced my niece in public, she has kept him at arm's length.
items.a: A — doesn't want to get close to Uche
items.why: Keeping someone at arm's length is maintaining distance from them.

items.q: If Seth really wants to be helped, he has to put his cards on the table.
items.a: B — has to be truthful, honest and frank
items.why: Putting one's cards on the table is disclosing everything openly.

items.q: We consider the day our daughter first went to school as a red-letter day.
items.a: A — of importance and therefore should be celebrated
items.why: A red-letter day is a memorable, important day.

items.q: When the officer challenged the order, the commander hit the ceiling.
items.why: To hit the ceiling is to explode with anger.

items.q: News of the chief's death spread like wildfire.
items.a: C — reached many people within a short time
items.why: Wildfire spreads uncontrollably fast — the point is speed and reach, not confusion.

items.q: It looks like Selina got out of bed on the wrong side.
items.a: D — was in a very bad mood
items.why: The idiom describes a bad temper from the start of the day.

items.q: James developed cold feet when he met the Manager to discuss his transfer.
items.a: B — had second thoughts about what he wanted to do
items.why: Cold feet means a loss of nerve — he hesitated rather than decided to change his mind.

items.q: The priest's death was a bolt from the blue.
items.why: A bolt from the blue is a complete surprise; the idiom says nothing about how he died.

items.q: Anne is two-faced in her interactions with her friends.
items.why: Two-faced means presenting different faces to different people.

items.q: When Joe got there, he decided to strike while the iron was hot.
items.a: D — took advantage of the situation
items.why: The idiom means acting promptly while the opportunity lasts.

items.q: Two months after moving into our new house, we hadn't noticed any ____ on the building …
items.why: Defects are faults in the structure; damages is not used in this count sense.

items.q: … till one Sunday morning when water started ____ from a corner of the shower …
items.why: The later sentence says water was "dropping heavily", and a small start is a drip.

items.q: … in our ____ bedroom.
items.why: The main bedroom of a house is the master bedroom.

items.q: We assumed it was a simple ____ and therefore asked my nephew … to fix it.
items.why: A leakage is the escape of water; that is the fault being fixed.

items.q: He did, but the ____ lasted for that day only.
items.why: The repair is what he carried out and what failed the next day.

items.q: Frantically, I called the ____ who promptly came to our rescue.
items.why: A plumber is the tradesman for water pipes and leaks.

items.q: A thorough check revealed that two roofing ____ had been blown away …
items.why: Roofing sheets are the panels that wind can lift; rafters and beams are the frame.

items.q: … causing water to collect on the ____.
items.why: Water from a damaged roof collects on the ceiling before it drips into the room.

items.q: The water therefore had to ____ through.
items.why: Seep means to pass slowly through a porous material.

items.q: We therefore had to re-roof that ____ of the house.
items.why: A house is re-roofed on a side; "phase" and "line" do not describe a part of a building.

items.why: Joe Gargery speaks this way throughout — the ungrammatical, affectionate voice is his signature.

items.q: Prose, Great Expectations: "…he hammered away at my mother" is an example of
items.why: Hammering is applied to beating a person, transferring the action of a hammer without using "like" or "as".

items.q: Prose, Great Expectations: What does the extract say about the persona? He was

items.q: Prose, Great Expectations: Biddy was

items.q: Prose, Great Expectations: The speaker was about to travel to

items.q: Prose, Great Expectations: Two other characters present were

items.q: Prose, Great Expectations: The speaker was thinking about the

items.why: He says morning "brightened" his "general prospect of life" — his thoughts are on what awaits him.

items.q: Prose, Great Expectations: The speaker was

items.q: Prose, Great Expectations: What is the meaning of "six days intervened between me and the day of departure"?

items.q: Prose, No Sweetness Here: Setu abhors the big men because they

items.q: Prose, No Sweetness Here: Setu and Zirigu are

items.q: Prose, No Sweetness Here: "Maybe it is better that all mothers are not like you…" — the speaker is

items.q: Prose, No Sweetness Here: The figure of speech in "the land would be flowing with the blood of all the big men" is
items.why: Blood is described as flowing like a river over the land — a comparison made without "like" or "as".

items.q: Prose, No Sweetness Here: What had occasioned this speech?
items.a: B — Immorality of the big men
items.why: The whole exchange is provoked by the conduct of wealthy men towards young girls.

items.q: Prose, No Sweetness Here: The mother referred to in the extract is

items.q: Prose, No Sweetness Here: "Please little sister, I am not trying to interfere in your private life…" — little sister refers to

items.q: Prose, No Sweetness Here: The speaker of that extract is
items.why: Connie is the elder sister who counsels Mercy in "Two Sisters".

items.q: Prose, No Sweetness Here: "That man" in the extract is
items.why: He is the already-attached man at the centre of the sisters' disagreement.

items.q: Drama, Merchant of Venice: "Mislike me not for my complexion…" — the speaker is
items.why: The Prince of Morocco opens his suit to Portia with exactly these lines.

items.q: Drama, Merchant of Venice: "The shadowed livery of the burnished sun" suggests the speaker
items.a: A — is at the mercy of the sun
items.why: He calls his dark skin the "livery" (uniform) the sun has imposed on him — the sun has marked him.

items.q: Drama, Merchant of Venice: The addressee is
items.why: Morocco is addressing the heiress he has come to woo.

items.q: Drama, Merchant of Venice: Which character was present at the scene?
items.why: Nerissa attends Portia throughout the casket scenes.

items.q: Drama, Merchant of Venice: One of the themes of the play is
items.why: The trial of Antonio turns entirely on the opposition between strict justice and mercy.

items.q: Drama, Merchant of Venice: "In Belmont is a lady richly left…" — these words were spoken
items.a: D — in a street in Venice
items.why: Bassanio speaks them to Antonio in Venice, describing Portia who lives in Belmont.

items.q: Drama, Merchant of Venice: To whom were these words spoken?
items.why: Bassanio is explaining to Antonio why he needs money to travel to Belmont.

items.q: Drama, Merchant of Venice: What is the meaning of "In Belmont is a lady richly left"?
items.a: A — A lady with substantial fortune lives in Belmont

subject: mathematics
label: WAEC Chief Examiner’s Report 2021 — Paper 2 walkthrough
note: Core Mathematics Paper 2, 2021. Question wording follows the examiner report; where the PDF's symbol font does not decode, the method and verified answer are given instead of a guessed formula.

items.q: Draw the multiplication ⊗ table in modulo 9 on {2, 3, 7, 8}, then use it to find the truth set of 8 ⊗ m = 2.
steps: Multiply each pair, then divide by 9 and keep the remainder.
Read across row 8 for the value 2: it occurs under m = 7.
items.tip: Write the answer as a set, {7} or {m : m = 7}. Candidates lost the mark for writing a bare "7".

items.q: X: All policemen wear uniform. Y: Civil servants do not wear uniform. With P = {policemen}, T = {people who wear uniform}, C = {civil servants}: (i) draw a Venn diagram; (ii) decide whether "Adu wears uniform ⇒ Adu is a policeman" and "Ofei is a policeman ⇒ Ofei is not a civil servant" are valid.
items.a: (i) P inside T; C entirely outside T. (ii) First implication: NOT valid. Second: VALID.
steps: X says every policeman is in the uniform set, so P ⊂ T.
Y says no civil servant is in T, so C and T do not overlap.
Adu wears uniform puts Adu in T — but T also contains people who are not policemen, so the first conclusion does not follow.
Ofei is a policeman, so Ofei ∈ P ⊂ T. Since C ∩ T = ∅, Ofei cannot be a civil servant.
The second implication therefore holds for every member of P.
items.tip: A conclusion is valid only if it must be true in every arrangement the premises allow — one counter-example kills it.

items.q: Given a relation connecting p, q and t, make t the subject, then find t when p = 2/3 and q = 3/4.
items.why: The examiner report prints the verified answer t = 1/20 and notes that part (a) was well answered.
steps: Clear fractions by multiplying both sides by the denominator.
Collect every term containing t on one side.
Factor out t: t(…) = (…), then divide by the bracket.
Substitute p = 2/3 and q = 3/4.
Simplify the resulting fraction to lowest terms.
items.tip: Before substituting, get t alone in a single tidy expression — substituting early usually creates messy arithmetic.

items.q: Given m and n as rational expressions in x, express (2m − n) in simplest form in terms of x.
items.why: The report attributes most lost marks here to failing to find the common denominator.
steps: Substitute the expressions for m and n into 2m − n.
Put every term over the common denominator (1 − x)(1 + x).
Expand the numerator carefully, keeping the minus sign on the whole of n.
Collect like terms; the numerator factors as 2x(1 + x).
Cancel the common factor (1 + x) with the denominator.
items.tip: When subtracting a fraction, bracket the whole numerator first — sign errors are the single biggest source of lost marks.

items.q: MNPR is a circle with centre O. The reflex angle at O is 204°, angle NRP = 52°, and angle MNP = m. Find m.
steps: The angle at the centre on the major arc is 360° − 204° = 156°.
Angle at the circumference on the same arc is half the angle at the centre: ∠MNP = 156° ÷ 2 = 78°.
Angles in triangle MNP: m + 204°? No — use the quadrilateral MNPR.
Sum of angles around the point and in the quadrilateral gives m + 204° + 78° + 52° = 360°.
items.tip: A reflex angle at the centre always pairs with the angle at the circumference on the *other* arc. Sketch both arcs before writing anything.

items.q: A 6.5 m ladder leans against a vertical wall with its top 3.6 m from the foot of the wall. Find the distance from the wall to the foot of the ladder.
steps: The wall, the ground and the ladder form a right-angled triangle with the ladder as hypotenuse.
Pythagoras: 6.5² = 3.6² + d².
items.tip: The ladder is always the hypotenuse — it is the longest side and opposite the right angle.

items.q: A cylindrical pipe is 210 cm long with external diameter 16 cm and wall thickness 1 cm. Find the volume of metal used. (π = 22/7)
items.why: Most candidates lost marks by using the diameter instead of the radius.
steps: External radius R = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm.
Internal radius r = 8 − 1 = 7 cm.
items.tip: "Thickness" subtracts from the radius, not the diameter. Halve first, then subtract.

items.q: M = (5, −7) and N = (0, 5). Calculate the distance MN.
steps: Distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
items.tip: Squaring removes the sign, so the order of subtraction does not matter — only be consistent.

items.q: Seven students scored in Physics and Mathematics. Calculate the Spearman rank correlation coefficient.
steps: Rank each subject separately (highest score = rank 1).
For each student find d = difference in ranks, then d².
Sum the d² column: Σd² = 20.
Apply rs = 1 − 6Σd² / [n(n² − 1)] with n = 7.
rs = 1 − 120/336 ≈ 0.64, indicating a fairly strong positive agreement.
items.tip: Rank both lists in the *same* direction before subtracting. Mixing ascending and descending destroys the sign of rs.

items.q: In a camp, 50 officers chose from beans, plantain and rice: 21 beans, 24 plantain, 18 rice; 3 beans only, 9 plantain only, 2 rice only; 5 chose all three. Find (i) plantain and beans only, (ii) exactly two kinds, (iii) none of the three.
steps: Let x = plantain and beans only, y = plantain and rice only, z = beans and rice only.
Plantain: 9 + x + y + 5 = 24 ⇒ x + y = 10.
Add all three: 2(x + y + z) = 34 ⇒ x + y + z = 17.
Exactly two = x + y + z = 6 + 4 + 7 = 17.
items.tip: Start from the centre region (all three), then fill the "exactly two" regions, and use each subject total to form an equation.

items.q: Copy and complete the table of values for y = 4 + 3x − 2x², for −4 ≤ x ≤ 4.
items.a: Values for x = −4…4 are obtained by direct substitution.
steps: Substitute each x into y = 4 + 3x − 2x².
items.tip: Square before multiplying by 2, and keep the minus sign attached to −2x².

items.q: Plot the graph using 2 cm to 1 unit on x and 2 cm to 5 units on y. From the graph find (i) the line of symmetry, (ii) the maximum point, (iii) values of x for which y decreases as x increases.
items.a: Line of symmetry x = 0.75; maximum point (0.75, 5.125); y decreases for x > 0.75.
items.why: The report notes that many candidates lost marks by using a scale other than the one specified.
steps: Plot the table points accurately and join with a smooth curve.
The line of symmetry passes through the turning point, parallel to the y-axis.
The curve opens downward (a < 0), so y decreases to the right of the maximum.
items.tip: Use exactly the scale given. A correct curve drawn to a different scale earns no marks for the follow-up readings.

items.q: A solid cylinder 6 m high and 28 cm in diameter is melted and recast into cylinders 14 cm high and 0.5 cm in diameter. How many smaller cylinders are obtained?
items.why: The report singles out unconverted units as the main reason candidates failed this question.
steps: Convert the big cylinder's height: 6 m = 600 cm.
Big radius = 28 ÷ 2 = 14 cm.
Small radius = 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 cm.
items.tip: Before any calculation, rewrite every length in the same unit. The π cancels, so it never needs a numerical value.

items.q: The unit digit of a two-digit number is 1 less than the tens digit. If the number is increased by 8 and divided by the sum of its digits, the result is 8. Find the number.
steps: Let the tens digit be x; the unit digit is x − 1.
The number is 10x + (x − 1) = 11x − 1.
Sum of digits = x + (x − 1) = 2x − 1.
Number increased by 8: 11x − 1 + 8 = 11x + 7.
Tens = 3, units = 2, so the number is 32. Check: (32 + 8) ÷ (3 + 2) = 40 ÷ 5 = 8. ✓
items.tip: Always substitute your final number back into the sentence. It catches both algebra slips and misread wording.

items.q: The ratio of cars to motorcycles sold is 5 : 7. If 142 more motorcycles than cars were sold, find the number of each.
steps: Let cars = 5k and motorcycles = 7k.
Difference = 7k − 5k = 2k = 142.
Motorcycles = 7 × 71 = 497.
items.tip: In a ratio question, the "difference" always corresponds to the difference of the ratio parts (7 − 5 = 2).

items.q: The probabilities of an athlete winning two independent events are 3/5 and 2/9. Find the probability of winning (i) only one event, (ii) none of the events.
steps: P(win first, lose second) = (3/5) × (7/9) = 21/45.
P(lose first, win second) = (2/5) × (2/9) = 4/45.
items.tip: "Only one" means exactly one — add the two orders and do not include the "both" case.

items.q: A cyclist goes from P on a bearing of 060° to Q, 5 km away, then on a bearing of 345° to R, 6 km from Q. (i) Draw the diagram. (ii) Find |PR| and the bearing of R from P.
items.a: |PR| ≈ 8.75 km; bearing of R from P ≈ 018.5°.
items.why: The report notes the diagram — not the calculation — was where most candidates failed.
steps: Sketch North at P and Q; mark 060° at P and 345° at Q.
The turn at Q gives an internal angle of 105° between QP and QR.
Cosine rule: PR² = 5² + 6² − 2(5)(6)cos 105°.
Sine rule: sin θ / 6 = sin 105° / 8.75 ⇒ sin θ ≈ 0.6625 ⇒ θ ≈ 41.5°.
Bearing of R from P = 60° − 41.5° = 018.5°.
items.tip: Draw the North line at every point. The internal angle of the triangle is rarely the bearing itself.

items.q: The values (x − 2), 4, (x + 2), (2x + 1), 9 are in order of size. If the median equals the mean, find x.
steps: There are 5 values, so the median is the 3rd: x + 2.
Check the ordering: 2, 4, 6, 9, 9 — genuinely in order. ✓
items.tip: When a question says values are "in order", use that as extra information — it confirms which value is the median.

items.q: Refuse in a community: 35% plastic, 27.5% liquid, 17.5% metal, 12.5% vegetable matter, 7.5% others. Draw a pie chart.
steps: Sector angle = percentage × 360°.
Check the angles sum to 360°.
items.tip: Always total the angles before drawing. If they do not sum to 360°, one percentage has been copied wrongly.

items.q: TP touches circle MNOP at P, MN is a diameter, angle MTP = 33° and angle PMN = 67°. Find angle MNT and angle MTN.
items.a: Solve using the tangent–chord and semicircle theorems; the report confirms candidates were expected to find ∠MNT = 67° and ∠MTN = 57°.
items.why: The diagram is an embedded image, so the exact lettering could not be transcribed. Follow the theorem sequence against your printed copy.
steps: MN is a diameter, so ∠MPN = 90° (angle in a semicircle).
TP is a tangent at P, so the angle between TP and the radius OP is 90°.
Angle between tangent and chord = angle in the alternate segment.
∠PMN = 67° is given; use the triangle MNP angle sum to reach ∠MPN's neighbours.
Carry the values around the circle one triangle at a time.
State each theorem by name as you use it — marks are awarded for the reason.
items.tip: For circle theorems, write the theorem name beside each step. Many marking schemes award a method mark for the theorem alone.

items.q: PQR is a circle with centre O. If angle QPR = 46°, find angle QOR.
steps: QPR is the angle at the circumference subtended by arc QR.
QOR is the angle at the centre subtended by the same arc.
Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference.
items.tip: Both angles must stand on the same arc. Identify the arc before applying the rule.

items.q: A train covers 120 km at average speed r. Technical problems reduce the speed by 5 km/h, increasing the scheduled time by 20 minutes. Find r.
steps: Scheduled time = 120/r hours.
Actual time = 120/(r − 5) hours.
Difference = 20 minutes = 1/3 hour.
Multiply through by 3r(r − 5): 360r − 360(r − 5) = r(r − 5).
items.tip: Convert every time to the same unit before forming the equation — 20 minutes is 1/3 hour, not 20.

items.q: g(x) = (3 + 5x)/(x − 3), x ≠ 3. Find (i) the image of −1, (ii) x when g(x) = 7, (iii) g(−3).
items.why: The examiner report prints g(x) = (3 + 5x)/(x − 3); the OCR shows the coefficient imperfectly.
items.tip: When solving g(x) = k, state the restriction x ≠ 3 — a root that makes the denominator zero must be rejected.

items.q: The sum of the first ten terms of an A.P. is 120. The fifth term is 6 less than the eighth term. Find the common difference and the first term.
steps: Fifth term = a + 4d; eighth term = a + 7d.
"6 less" gives a + 4d = a + 7d − 6.
Check: terms 3, 5, 7, …; fifth = 11, eighth = 17, difference 6. ✓
items.tip: Translate "6 less than" as "= other − 6", not "− 6 = other". Direction is the most common A.P. error.
